blocks.h1: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.heading: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.text: Céline’s song is called *On ne change pas*—“we don’t change.” I think that’s basically true. You grow up, but the child is still there. Sometimes adult life hits the exact place where you still feel small, abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.
blocks.authorship_evidence: current review assembly; not independent authorship proof
blocks.known_context_note: Opening component/assembly evidence differs; cumulative file retains unresolved full-opening watch.

blocks.h1: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.heading: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.text: So I stopped asking the child to heal itself. I started being the grown-up instead—the Nurturer, Protector, and Leader or Guide.
blocks.authorship_evidence: current review assembly; not independent authorship proof
blocks.known_context_note: Opening component/assembly evidence differs; cumulative file retains unresolved full-opening watch.

blocks.h1: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.heading: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.text: But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem. What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult? This is much easier when you can already reach one of those adult roles. But when you can't, it's like you sit there trying to be loving while your mind is becoming controlled again by the inherited critic voice, or you start going numb, throwing a fit, or panicking.
blocks.authorship_evidence: current review assembly; not independent authorship proof
blocks.known_context_note: Opening component/assembly evidence differs; cumulative file retains unresolved full-opening watch.

blocks.h1: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.heading: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.text: Sometimes somebody else may have to do one part of the adult role with you or for you first. You get to feel what that is like and watch how they do it. Maybe you copy one small thing you've seen them do, or imagine them there when they're not, and try one piece yourself while they're still helping with the rest. That's what I mean by borrowed adulthood. You may still need help with almost all of it for a while, but over time there are more and more of those little parts you can do yourself.
blocks.authorship_evidence: current review assembly; not independent authorship proof

blocks.h1: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.heading: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.text: For now, I think of it in five fairly predictable stages. You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):
blocks.authorship_evidence: current review assembly; not independent authorship proof
blocks.known_context_note: Opening component/assembly evidence differs; cumulative file retains unresolved full-opening watch.

blocks.h1: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.heading: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
blocks.text:
1. You're still fully identified as the child — use your childlike superpowers to come into the "Wow of Now" (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there's enough safety around you to continue:
2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we're looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you'd take care of a baby doll etc. 
3. Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.
4. Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them. 
5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn't pushed away, but doesn't have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you've been stuck in adult mode for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!
blocks.authorship_evidence: current review assembly; not independent authorship proof

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: My Journey
blocks.text: I used to preach [Buddhist enlightenment](http://mindset.u-dont-exist.com/) a lot. But an old childhood wound could still hit and suddenly I was the same little kid again, even when the spiritual part of me felt completely free.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: My Journey
blocks.text: The way I picture it is almost stupidly simple. Imagine you're broke and starving, and your baby is starving too. *Understandable*: there is no food. Then a food bank opens nearby and suddenly you've got lots of nutritious munchies. But you're eating all of it yourself while baby you is still starving. *Unforgivable.*
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: My Journey
blocks.text: Nobody leaves a baby starving on purpose. I just didn't believe there was a baby. Inner-child stuff sounded silly to me until I could actually feel him. Then there was this little me actually hurting, and I could send some of the love I'd already found his way.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: My Journey
blocks.text: I think most people who chase spiritual freedom are also trying to get away from something painful in themselves, and a lot of it goes back to childhood. That's [spiritual bypassing](https://goenka.u-dont-exist.com/). Plenty of seekers and gurus do it too; I've written about the [Dalai Lama as one example](https://substack.com/@udontexist/note/c-245314772?r=5vdc6m). I did it too. It doesn't mean you're stupid or crazy.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: My Journey
blocks.text: Spending your whole life processing the wounded kid isn't freedom either. Spirituality opened a much bigger horizon for me—love and happiness beyond the conditions of my life story. Maybe ordinary life already gives you enough love and meaning. Great. It didn't for me. Conditional love felt radically insufficient, so I kept looking for something deeper.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: If you still feel like a kid inside, somebody who seems grown-up can feel like salvation, and handing them the steering wheel can actually help for a while. But they can know things you don't and still be wrong about you.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: Even [Pema Chödrön](https://pemachodronfoundation.org/product/taking-the-leap-book/) comes from a tradition where devotion to a teacher is a big deal, and she still says a teacher should “wean us from dependency altogether” and help us grow up.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: If you're actually in danger, maybe you need to get out or get some help, even if meditation is helping with the pain. Calling it “your story” doesn't protect the kid from what's happening.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: Say you grew up learning that what you wanted didn't matter. Now you're only just finding out what you actually think, maybe even learning to say no. Then somebody tells you there is no self. That might be freeing at another point in your life; right now it can sound a lot like the message you already know: what you want doesn't matter. Or you tell a therapist, “No, that's not right for me,” and they call it resistance. Maybe they're right. But maybe they're wrong about you, or taking you somewhere you don't want to go. You still have to be able to say so.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: Borrow adulthood. Do not surrender it.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: My own case was weird. I was well-loved as a child, but from age twelve to twenty-six I was depressed and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world. [Loving-kindness (metta) meditation](http://love.u-dont-exist.com/) healed that depression almost instantly for me.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: I wasn't lacking love. My parents had given me a lot of it. I found more in [Buddhist teachings—which, it turns out, also include inner-child self-love!](https://substack.com/profile/355021294-u-dont-existcom/note/c-297324975) and later in [loveyhuasca](http://soma.u-dont-exist.com/). Metta gave all that love somewhere to land.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: But it didn't reach everything. A lot of the child stuff around my attachment to women was still there. When I later tried [self-directed inner-child therapy](https://youtu.be/yEWFjODXJbI?si=IXUqrhExojOm6Itm), it felt like I was making it up at first. I used San Pedro cactus and CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, and that cracked it open; structured sessions with an inner-child therapist deepened it.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: My Journey
blocks.heading: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
blocks.text: Sometimes I'd get past a protective part and reach the child, then get pulled so far into being him that there wasn't a grown-up me around anymore. The three adult jobs from the map don't work too well when the adult has vanished, so I started looking for a way to have an adult there before I could reliably be that adult myself.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner-grounded memoir/reflection with model editing; accepted/good-enough current wording

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
blocks.text: If you don't hear a little kid talking in your head, don't invent one. Actually, this is one place where the usual inner-child prompt can get confusing, because “ask” sounds like you're supposed to ask a question and then wait for a second voice to answer. Maybe that's what happens for some people, but you might not be some people.
blocks.authorship_evidence: protected owner-final subsection; paragraph-level authorship not newly adjudicated

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
blocks.text: You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and yet still be able to think a sentence on purpose. Try it and see. If words are there, speak or write them. You might feel more comfortable that way than just staying in imagination land.  And if that starts feeling like homework you're doing for a child who isn't answering, drop it. Maybe what's actually requiring your attention now is a knot in your stomach. Or perhaps you're in a place you want to leave. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be nice to do for yourself.
blocks.authorship_evidence: protected owner-final subsection; paragraph-level authorship not newly adjudicated

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
blocks.text: And it might not be the same order all the time. You could have a feeling before thoughts, or thoughts might come first and provoke a feeling. They say hindsight is 20/20, but you actually might not even know which happened first. That's ok, too.
blocks.authorship_evidence: protected owner-final subsection; paragraph-level authorship not newly adjudicated

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
blocks.text: You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns you: you're supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Pema Chödrön calls this tightening and urge before the story has finished forming, "shenpa." Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute. You can figure that out later.
blocks.authorship_evidence: protected owner-final subsection; paragraph-level authorship not newly adjudicated

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
blocks.text: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: "Oh! I'm hooked again! That's awesome I could notice it!" If nobody is in danger, take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Sometimes human beings need to be being, not always doing. 🙃 Maybe then you'll find there's enough adult around to be nice to the kid for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you'd regret later.
blocks.authorship_evidence: protected owner-final subsection; paragraph-level authorship not newly adjudicated

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
blocks.text: Here's where I want to clearly depart from the new age wisdom that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary and still have hit something old in you. You felt your stomach tighten up, and that somehow meant “They're evil.” But you can defer that judgement for when you're in your happy place.
blocks.authorship_evidence: protected owner-final subsection; paragraph-level authorship not newly adjudicated

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Also Look Outward
blocks.text: Have you ever had a fight where you were absolutely sure you'd finally seen who somebody was, and then they came back later and had a basically normal conversation with you? Irritating. They can still disagree with you. Their boundary can still make you mad. Now the first fight has company. What matters more is when the subject changes but somehow you keep ending up in the same role: taking care of their reaction while your own experience disappears. [Lindsay Gibson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) writes about those repeated relational patterns in her work on emotional immaturity.
blocks.authorship_evidence: model realization in previously accepted mixed subsection; individual detector status must remain separate
blocks.known_context_note: Prior combined subsection Human result does not certify this paragraph.

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Also Look Outward
blocks.text: You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they. If they promise to change, that's probably as useful as their prior promises were. Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy. Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise? Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.
blocks.authorship_evidence: direct owner paragraph

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Also Look Outward
blocks.text: If you really did hurt them, repair it.

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Also Look Outward
blocks.text: You can mean the apology. Then notice what happens next. Are you sorry for what you did, or are you starting to take back the complaint too because they're still upset? Maybe your first explanation sucked. Try again. But if you've said what you mean and said no, you can't guarantee they'll understand it. Guilt may keep shouting at you. That doesn't tell you the whole conflict was yours, and it doesn't prove they're manipulating you.

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
blocks.text: Yeah, I mean, this happens all the time. I'll be writing out a reply to someone and, if I'm doing good, I might suddenly think, wait, that's not the best way to put it. It's not like I'm suppressing my feelings; I'm expressing them in a way that can be heard. It's actually way easier to do this with texts than with speaking, of course, but texts are good practice. Owning anything I did wrong is the tricky part because often what I did wrong was mostly just not being very high-IQ and high-EQ in how I communicated. If I actually did do something I know was wrong aside from that, it's easier for me at least. It can be hard to apologize for just being too direct because I associate that with honesty at some level.
blocks.authorship_evidence: owner rough cognition preserved near-verbatim for a humanization experiment; Pangram Human 1.0; not owner-final article prose

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
blocks.text: It doesn't mean you need to hide your upset, or apply for a permit to protest, but choose your battles and execute them wisely, so you don't end up regretting how you communicated later. As Lao Tsu might have said (if I could ever have read that whole boring Art of War book), a war with no casualties is the best possible war. When high IQ & EQ communication hits a writer's block, sometimes the best thing is to simply say, "I need some time to think about my response." And if the conflict really requires a response right now, then obviously just do your best rather than wait for the perfect timing.
blocks.authorship_evidence: direct owner paragraph
blocks.known_context_note: Owner-reported Human/medium; no redundant raw-owner control purchased.

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.text: First check whether there's enough grown-up you around to do this right now. Can you look around the room, pause before acting, and make a choice you can actually follow through on? If you're basically the frightened kid and those things have gone offline, skip the deep dive. Get somebody steady around you or do what helps you come back a bit. You can talk to the child later.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Maybe Calm the Body First
blocks.text: Sometimes the problem isn't words at all. You're just too tense to get anywhere with the conversation.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Maybe Calm the Body First
blocks.text: If your solar plexus, abdomen, or somewhere else feels clenched and it's hard to relax into that heart-chakra love, try a slower, non-forced exhale or some gentle massage. I love using one foot to massage the other like a Yin/Yang symbol. Circular or spiral massage over the tense area can be nice too.
blocks.authorship_evidence: model paragraph with an explicit source-derived owner massage example; not an all-model thought control

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Maybe Calm the Body First
blocks.text: Sometimes you need more bottom-up help than that: Shaking, tapping (Emotional Freedom Technique), EMDR, Brainspotting, Somatic Experiencing, Water Therapy, Massage, Energy Healing, or another approach that works from the body upward.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Maybe Calm the Body First
blocks.text: Order matters. If the body is still freaking out, conversation can wait. That's what the roadmap below is for.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: Maybe Calm the Body First
blocks.text: If you close your eyes and start losing the actual room, open them again. Look around. Know where you are and what time it is. Feel your body here. If these sessions leave you more disoriented, more compelled, or less able to function afterward, shorten them and get some grounded support instead of trying to win a contest with your own nervous system.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: When Healing Turns Into Checking
blocks.text: You can get hooked on healing too. The wound can be completely real while you're checking it for the hundredth time to see whether you've finally grieved it correctly.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: When Healing Turns Into Checking
blocks.text: Handle whatever safety issue or practical thing actually needs doing. Then, before another round, ask what changed the last time you processed this. Did you finally feel something you had only been thinking about? Did you notice something new enough to change a decision or how you respond? Or are you asking the same question again because the answer didn't feel certain enough? Grief can come back to familiar ground. Repetition by itself doesn't mean the child has a new request.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: When Healing Turns Into Checking
blocks.text: If it's checking, let the thought stay there without arguing with it or trying to make it disappear, and go back to the person, activity, or life you chose. You do not have to wait until it feels completely resolved. Caring for the child does not require holding a meeting every time your mind produces a sentence.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: When Healing Turns Into Checking
blocks.text: Before doing the same exercise again, know what it is supposed to help and what would actually look different if it were working. You can leave a session calmer and full of insight while the original problem doesn't move at all. If the method keeps giving you no useful contact—or mostly makes you monitor yourself more while daily life gets worse—don't answer that by doing more of it. Keep what genuinely helps and try another way of meeting the same need.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5

blocks.h1: Before You Try to Go Deep
blocks.heading: When Healing Turns Into Checking
blocks.text: If these exercises start feeling like a ritual you have to complete before you're allowed to live, stop there.
blocks.authorship_evidence: unresolved model realization from frozen R5
